Idioms.phrase: When it rains, it pours - Lots of things are causing difficulties or going wrong at the same time.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, First the photocopier broke, and now her desk chair is wobbling. Everything seems to be going wrong this morning! When it rains, it pours!

Idioms.phrase: When pigs fly - Something that will never happen.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Are you serious? That's never going to happen. Maybe when pigs fly!

Idioms.phrase: When push comes to shove - When it becomes necessary to act.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My brother might seem a bit flaky sometimes, but he's always there for me when push comes to shove.

Idioms.phrase: When the chips are down - When things aren't going well.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Helen is always there for her friends when the chips are down. She never fails them in difficult situations.

Idioms.phrase: Where the rubber meets the road - A critical moment or turning point in an endeavor.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Ben had been nervous about the basketball championships for months. Tomorrow was the day. It was time for the rubber to meet the road.

Idioms.phrase: Where were we? - What were we talking about/doing?
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Where we were in our conversation before we were interrupted?

Idioms.phrase: White elephant - A possession that is costly but fundamentally useless.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The family's new gazebo ended up being something of a white elephant. They spent a fortune on it and they never use it.

Idioms.phrase: White lie - A slight lie or exaggeration, or a lie that doesn't do any harm.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Though Anna didn't tell the truth, she claimed it was only a white lie. What she said hadn’t hurt anyone.

Idioms.phrase: Whitewash - To try to cover up something bad.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Everything seemed okay at first, but then we discovered that the real situation had been whitewashed.

Idioms.phrase: Who asked you? - No one asked you, so why are you offering an opinion?
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Who asked you? I don't want your opinion on my jacket.

Idioms.phrase: Who do you think you are? - Why do you think you're entitled to say/do that?
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I can't believe you would say something so arrogant. Who do you think you are?

Idioms.phrase: Whole ball of wax – Everything, or all things, involved in something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She took part in all kinds of extracurricular activities at college. Debate society, basketball, track and field. The whole ball of wax.

Idioms.phrase: Wild and woolly - Untamed and wild.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Did you see Adam today? He was looking a bit wild and woolly, wasn't he?

Idioms.phrase: Will take place - Will occur.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The awards ceremony will take place two weeks from today.

Idioms.phrase: Wine and dine - To treat someone to an expensive meal.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, David had a crush on Deanna. He wanted to take her out so that he could wine and dine her.

Idioms.phrase: Winging it - Doing something in the absence of preparation, planning, or some special knowledge.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It doesn’t seem like he's completely sure of what he's doing. He seems to be winging it while he tries to figure it out.

Idioms.phrase: With bated breath - To feel a great sense of anticipation or expectation (could be positive or negative).
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She waited for her exam results with bated breath.

Idioms.phrase: With bells on - With enthusiasm, usually when attending an event.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Anthony said that he was really excited about the upcoming festival and that he'd be there with bells on!

Idioms.phrase: With flying colors - To do something extremely well.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Adam passed the exam with flying colors! He got an A+.

Idioms.phrase: Wolf in sheep's clothing - Someone who has the appearance of being good but who actually has negative or bad intentions.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They thought that he would be a good business partner, but he turned out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing.

Idioms.phrase: Work against the clock - To work on something that you probably won't get done in time.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We were working against the clock to get the project done on time.

Idioms.phrase: Worth one's salt - Competent at what one does.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It took a while for the boss to decide whether or not his new employee was worth his salt.

Idioms.phrase: Wouldn't be caught dead - Would never want to do something, probably because it would cause embarrassment.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Maria hated the new blue sweater that her parents had bought her. She thought it looked terrible on her and told her friends that she wouldn't be caught dead in it.

Idioms.phrase: Wouldn't hurt a fly - Very gentle and unable, or unlikely, to ever hurt anyone or anything.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don’t worry about her. She wouldn't hurt a fly; she’s very gentle.

Idioms.phrase: Wouldn't touch it with a ten-foot pole - Would never even think about coming anywhere close to it or becoming involved with it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Frank and Ashley agreed about the open position at the company down the road. They wouldn't touch it with a ten-foot pool. Neither would be applying.

Idioms.phrase: Wrap your head around something - To understand a complex subject.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I didn't understand how to solve the math problem. I just couldn't seem to wrap my head around it.

Idioms.phrase: X marks the spot - To have found what one was looking for.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Here it is! The notebook I was looking for. X marks the spot!

Idioms.phrase: You bet - That's right, I will, or I agree.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You bet! I'd love to come with you tomorrow.

Idioms.phrase: You can bet your boots - I think it's definitely true.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You can bet your boots that it's true! I'm absolutely sure of it.

Idioms.phrase: You can bet your bottom dollar - You can be certain.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You can bet your bottom dollar that Ethan's new business will do well. He's an incredibly hard worker and there is demand in the area for his services.

Idioms.phrase: You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make him drink - You cannot compel another person to make the right decision.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I tried to convince Brooke that she would do better in the other course, but she wouldn't listen. It's true, you know. You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make him drink.

Idioms.phrase: You can say that again - I agree or that is true.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You can say that again! I agree that the weather was terrible.

Idioms.phrase: You can't have your cake and eat it too - It's impossible to have everything.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Margaret was frustrated that she couldn't afford to buy both tops at once, but she realized that you can't have your cake and eat it too.

Idioms.phrase: You can't judge a book by its cover - You shouldn't try to judge someone or something just by how it looks.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He thought that his teacher looked like she might be mean, but people told him that he shouldn't judge a book by its cover.

Idioms.phrase: You can't make an omelet without breaking some eggs - There are always costs involved when accomplishing something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Some people were upset about the costs of the endeavor. We just had to remind them that you can't make an omelet without breaking some eggs.

Idioms.phrase: You can't squeeze blood out of a turnip - You cannot get something out of nothing.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Matt was really frustrated at how people were demanding that he pay the money he owed. He told them that he didn't have the funds, and that you can't squeeze blood out of a turnip.

Idioms.phrase: You can't take it with you - No matter how much money or how many material possessions you have, you can't take them with you when you die.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The couple decided to go on a world cruise. It was very expensive, but they didn’t mind. After all, you can't take it with you.

Idioms.phrase: You can't teach an old dog new tricks - It's harder for an older person to learn new information.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He was nervous about going back to school because of people telling him that you can't teach an old dog new tricks. He did really well, though!

Idioms.phrase: You get what you pay for - If you buy something very cheap, you cannot complain about it being low quality.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I know you're frustrated about the stitches coming loose on your new top, but you get what you pay for. It was very cheap.

Idioms.phrase: You'll catch more flies with honey than with vinegar - Being nice will make it easier to get what you want.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Some people wonder why I'm always so nice to Jack, when he’s so difficult and uncooperative. But I always say that you'll catch more flies with honey than with vinegar.

Idioms.phrase: Your guess is as good as mine - I don't have the information needed to know the answer.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Did you ask what the weather will be like tomorrow? Your guess is as good as mine.

Idioms.phrase: You're telling me - That's obviously true.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You're telling me! There’s no way that huge diamond is real.

Idioms.phrase: You've sold me - You have convinced me.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Okay, I'll go to the concert with you. You've sold me on it. It sounds like it will be a lot of fun.

Idioms.phrase: Zero tolerance - Refusal to tolerate something at all.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The school has a zero tolerance policy when it comes to any sort of violence.

Idioms.phrase: Zip it - Be quiet.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Our teacher lost his patience. He told one of the loudest students to zip it.
